said: Coals still alive under the ash. Tinder on them, blow, and it takes.

journal.text: A day's proper work behind me and my arms know it. Fish trap's in the water, two snares laid along the warren path, wood stacking up on the rack before the weather turns. Best of it though: I set scraps out for the dog and backed off, and she came and ate them, watching me the whole time like I might change my mind about being harmless. Didn't try to touch her — that's a day for another time. Still just the two of us out here, but it feels a little less like just the one.

Third day, and I made it through a hungry night without it turning into anything worse. Whatever I managed between the trap, the snares and what's left in my hands has quieted my stomach, if not answered every question about tomorrow. Fire's out again — that's twice now, and I'm getting tired of relighting it from scratch each morning. Fog's thick enough I can't see the shore from the lean-to. Feeling the quiet of this place more today than I have — no one to grumble to about any of it but myself, and Nell, who isn't much for conversation yet. Fire first, then the woodpile cover, then I'll see what the fog gives up.

Second shelter done today — a proper debris hut, ridge and ribs and a deep bed of leaves, built with my own two hands and whatever the wood gave me. Fire's lit again and holding, third time of asking. I'm wrung out in a way that's more satisfaction than exhaustion, if that makes any sense to anyone but me. Tomorrow there's still that third snare wanting a noose, and the woodpile could do with its cover before the weather changes its mind about being kind. For now I'll sit by the fire a while and let my hands rest.

Fourth day, and hunger's caught up with me properly — weak enough this morning that the berry bushes swam a bit before my eyes. I've been so set on the building that I've let the eating slide, and that's a fool's bargain out here. The trap and the snares haven't given me much yet, whatever the reason, so it's berries and whatever else I can find with my own two hands today. No more roofs, no more tripods, till I've put something solid back in my stomach. Nell was watching from the treeline again this morning — I daresay she knows hunger better than I do.

Sat by the fire tonight and counted up what's done: lean-to, fire ring, signal tripod, fish trap, all three snares, the debris hut, and now the woodpile with its cover. Four days, and everything I set my mind to that first hungry night is built and standing. I ought to feel like a man who's won something. Instead it's the quiet that's got me — proper lonely tonight, more than I've let on. Nell's closer than she was, and I'm glad of her, but she's not much for talking back. Tomorrow I think I'll walk further than I have — see more of this place than the same worn paths between hut and fire and trap. A man needs something ahead of him, not just behind.

Fifth day, and I've been properly ill overnight — cramping, sweating, up more than once. I keep turning it over: was it the berries, the stream water, or that marsh water I had a bad feeling about even as I drank it? Can't say for certain, and that not-knowing is its own kind of misery. What I do know is I've been careless about water since I got here, telling myself a sailor's stomach can take anything, and a sailor's stomach very much cannot. From now on it's boiled water only, whatever the bother of it. Weak and hungry again this morning too — desperately so — which doesn't help me tell illness from hunger. Very low today, if I'm honest with this page. Nell came close enough to nose at my hand while I lay there, which I won't forget in a hurry.

lastThought: Hungry again, proper hungry, same as every night this week near enough. Three snares and a trap and it's still not steady. Maybe what I need isn't more of the same but new ground — further along the coast, past what I've already picked clean.
